name: Rayon
listed_description: Rust data-parallelism library with a work-stealing thread pool; turning iter() into par_iter() parallelises a loop, comparable in ease to OpenMP, TBB or ConCRT parallel for.
claim_text: The book says par_iter gives ease of use similar to C++ parallel for constructs; no timings are given.
book_benchmark: None. Only a qualitative comparison to OpenMP, Microsoft ConCRT and Intel TBB parallel loops, and an explanation of work stealing.
guessed_baseline: OpenMP parallel for / Intel oneTBB parallel_for / std::execution::par
found_in: book: Rust for C++ Developers (2026), ch. 11 Multithreading in Rust, sections Thread pooling and Parallel iterators with Rayon

name: rust-brotli (Dropbox Rust port of Brotli)
listed_description: Book mentions, without naming the project, a 2016 team port of Brotli from C to Rust whose speed improved after removing buffer initialization and bounds checks. Repo identified as the likely match from its README (direct port of the C compressor).
claim_text: After removing expensive initialization and bounds checking, the Rust Brotli port improved by over 10 percent (it had first been slower than C).
book_benchmark: No benchmark shown by the book; anecdote about a 2016 C to Rust port. Compiler, flags and CPU not stated. The improvement is Rust-with-unsafe versus the same port with checks, so it measures the port against itself.
found_in: book: Rust for C++ Developers (2026), ch. 10 Optimization in Rust, section Initialization and bounds checking

name: Rust matrix multiply: accumulator hoisted into a local sum
listed_description: Naive triple-loop f32 matrix multiply over Vec<Vec<f32>> rewritten to accumulate the inner product in a local variable and store once per output cell (function matrix_multiply_indexing_opt in chapter_10).
claim_text: 100x100 multiply dropped from about 2.24 ms to about 540 microseconds, a 75.9 percent improvement.
book_benchmark: Criterion benchmark, 100x100 f32 matrices, release build, Rust 1.82.0 or newer, author's own machine (CPU not stated). Baseline is the book's own naive version; first-party.
guessed_baseline: naive nested-loop matrix multiply with in-place accumulation (same language)
found_in: book: Rust for C++ Developers (2026), ch. 10 Optimization in Rust, section Measuring the performance of Rust programs > Benchmarking

name: Rust matrix multiply: get_unchecked bounds-check removal
listed_description: Same f32 matrix multiply with unsafe get_unchecked and get_unchecked_mut in the inner loop to drop bounds checks (function matrix_multiply_unsafe_indexing in chapter_10).
claim_text: 100x100 multiply went from about 540 microseconds to about 359 microseconds, a 33.7 percent improvement over the previous step.
book_benchmark: Criterion benchmark, 100x100 f32, release build, Rust 1.82.0 or newer, author's machine (CPU not stated). Baseline is the book's own safe indexed version; first-party.
guessed_baseline: safe bounds-checked indexed matrix multiply (same language)
found_in: book: Rust for C++ Developers (2026), ch. 10 Optimization in Rust, section Improving performance using unsafe Rust code > Removing bounds checks

name: Rust matrix multiply: std::simd f32x4 inner product
listed_description: Matrix multiply inner loop processing four f32 values at a time with std::simd f32x4 plus swizzle-based horizontal add, nightly Rust only (src/simd.rs in chapter_10).
claim_text: 100x100 multiply improved by about 41 percent to roughly 208 microseconds versus the scalar unsafe-indexing version.
book_benchmark: Criterion benchmark via cargo +nightly bench, 100x100 f32, author's machine (CPU not stated). Baseline is the book's own scalar unsafe version; b matrix not transposed; sizes must be multiples of four.
found_in: book: Rust for C++ Developers (2026), ch. 10 Optimization in Rust, section Optimizing with SIMD instructions > Writing a SIMD function

name: Rust portable SIMD (std::simd / portable-simd)
listed_description: Rust's portable, cross-architecture SIMD API (Simd<T, N>), unstable and nightly-only; book likens it to Intel ISPC for avoiding per-architecture intrinsics.
claim_text: Book calls SIMD the gold standard for CPU compute and shows a roughly 41 percent speedup from std::simd in its matrix multiply.
book_benchmark: Only the matrix multiply example above (f32x4, 100x100, Criterion, author's machine) against a scalar loop.
guessed_baseline: std::arch / platform intrinsics, scalar loops, or C++ std::experimental::simd / xsimd
found_in: book: Rust for C++ Developers (2026), ch. 10 Optimization in Rust, section Optimizing with SIMD instructions > Setting up nightly Rust

name: packed_simd
listed_description: Nightly-only Rust crate with an API very similar to std::simd; book names it as an alternative but does not use it.
found_in: book: Rust for C++ Developers (2026), ch. 10 Optimization in Rust, section Setting up nightly Rust
